The cosmic language describes the passing of the old covenant “heavens and earth”, the whole Mosaic order, which ended in AD 70. Full preterists link this with Hebrews 12:26–28 and 2 Peter 3, which they also apply to that event.

These are real signs in the heavens at the end of the future tribulation, preceding Christ's visible return, and they match Revelation 6:12–14 and Joel 2:30–31. The word “immediately” (eutheōs) means the coming follows the tribulation directly, which is impossible if the tribulation was in AD 70 and the coming still future; therefore the tribulation itself must be future.

Futurists argue that the prophets' cosmic language, while used of local judgments, ultimately points to the final day of the Lord on the whole world (Isaiah 13:9–11; Isaiah 24; Joel 3:15–16), which Jesus now places at his return. Luke's “distress of nations” and the roaring sea suggest a universal crisis.

Ladd and others take the cosmic signs as real disturbances at the end of the age, though expressed in traditional prophetic language. They stress that 24:29 places the coming after the tribulation, which supports a posttribulational return.

The language may be both symbolic and anticipatory: symbolic of God's shaking of earthly powers, as in AD 70, and pointing to the final cosmic renewal at Christ's return (2 Peter 3:10–13). Many amillennialists read 24:29–31 as the final coming, with “immediately” expressing prophetic perspective rather than chronological sequence.

Adventist historicists traditionally applied the darkening of the sun and moon to the Dark Day in New England (19 May 1780) and the falling stars to the great Leonid meteor shower of 13 November 1833, coming after the papal persecution was “shortened”, with the Lisbon earthquake of 1755 as a preceding sign (Revelation 6:12–13).
Cosmic language for the fall of nations

Isaiah uses darkened sun, moon and stars for Babylon's fall (13:10) and dissolving heavens and falling stars for Edom's (34:4); Ezekiel uses it for Pharaoh (32:7–8). These were historical judgments carried out by armies.
Portents in the sky

Josephus reports a star like a sword and a comet that remained for a year, and chariots and armed troops seen running through the clouds around the cities; Tacitus says armies were seen clashing in the sky and the temple lit by fire from the clouds.
“Immediately after”

Futurists argue that eutheōs ties the cosmic signs and the coming tightly to the tribulation. If the coming in 24:30–31 is future, the tribulation must be too; if the tribulation was AD 70, the coming must have been AD 70, a conclusion most Christians reject.
The final cosmic renewal
The New Testament elsewhere uses similar imagery for the end of the present creation (2 Peter 3:10–13; Revelation 6:12–17; 20:11), suggesting that Jesus' words also look to the end of the world.
Whether the cosmic signs are prophetic metaphor for political and covenantal collapse in AD 70, or literal events at the end of history, and what “immediately after” requires.
The sign of the Son of Man and the coming on the clouds

“Then will appear in heaven the sign of the Son of Man, and then all the tribes of the earth (or land) will mourn, and they will see the Son of Man coming on the clouds of heaven with power and great glory.”

The words combine Daniel 7:13–14, where “one like a son of man” comes with the clouds to the Ancient of Days and receives dominion, and Zechariah 12:10–14, where the tribes of the land mourn for the one they pierced. In the Old Testament God “rides on a swift cloud” to judge Egypt (Isaiah 19:1; compare Psalm 18:9–12; 104:3; Nahum 1:3) without being physically seen. The Greek gē can mean earth or land, and phylai (tribes) usually refers to the tribes of Israel.

In Daniel 7:13 the Son of Man comes up to the Ancient of Days to receive his kingdom, not down to earth. Jesus uses the image for his vindication and enthronement, made visible when the temple that rejected him was destroyed: the “sign” is that the Son of Man is in heaven, reigning. The tribes of the land, Israel, mourn as Zechariah foretold, and the high priest would “see” this (26:64). France, Wright and Gentry take this view; earlier writers such as Thomas Newton and J. Stuart Russell also applied the passage to AD 70.

This coming in the clouds was the parousia, fulfilled in AD 70 as a coming in judgment, as in Isaiah 19:1. Since Jesus' contemporaries were told they would see it (26:64), there is no future coming in the clouds left to await.

This is the visible, bodily Second Coming at the end of the tribulation, when Christ descends to the Mount of Olives (Zechariah 14:4; Acts 1:11) and all the nations see him. Revelation 1:7 combines Daniel 7:13 and Zechariah 12:10 the same way and applies them to a universal event (“every eye will see him”).

Historic premillennialists read this as the one visible, posttribulational return of Christ, the event Paul describes in 1 Thessalonians 4:16–17 and 2 Thessalonians 1:7–10, when the church will meet the Lord.

Most amillennialists read 24:30 as the final return of Christ in glory, following AD 70 and the age-long tribulation; some allow that the Daniel 7 imagery is fulfilled first in the enthronement and judgment of AD 70 and finally at the Second Coming.

The Son of Man's coming on the clouds is first his enthronement at the right hand of God, displayed throughout history whenever his judgments fall, and finally his visible return. The church lives under the reign already established.

The sign of the Son of Man in heaven is the revelation of the risen Christ seated in glory, and those who mourn are those who come to see the one they pierced. His coming is the unveiling of who he is, which every believer is called to see by faith.
Daniel 7:13 is an ascent to God

In Daniel the Son of Man comes to the Ancient of Days and is given dominion (7:13–14). R. T. France argues that Jesus applies this to his vindication and authority after his rejection, which he says the high priest and his contemporaries will witness “from now on” (26:64).
God's cloud-comings in judgment

The Old Testament speaks of the Lord riding on a swift cloud and coming to Egypt in judgment (Isaiah 19:1), and of his coming on clouds against nations (Psalm 18:9–12; Nahum 1:3), events carried out through human armies.
Acts 1:11 and Revelation 1:7

The angels promise that Jesus will come in the same way he was seen going into heaven, in a cloud; Revelation 1:7 says every eye will see him. Futurists argue that this personal, visible coming is the natural meaning of Matthew 24:30.
Earth or land?

“All the tribes of the earth” (pasai hai phylai tēs gēs) can be translated “all the tribes of the land”, echoing Zechariah 12:12–14, which favours Israel; but the same phrase in Genesis 12:3 and 28:14 (LXX) refers to all the families of the earth.
Whether the coming on the clouds is a heavenly enthronement and judgment seen in AD 70, or the visible, bodily return of Christ to earth.
Angels gather the elect

“He will send out his angels with a loud trumpet call, and they will gather his elect from the four winds, from one end of heaven to the other.” Luke instead tells the disciples to lift up their heads, because their redemption is drawing near.

The verse echoes Deuteronomy 30:4 (God gathering exiled Israel from the ends of heaven), Zechariah 2:6 (the four winds), and Isaiah 27:13 (a great trumpet gathering exiles to worship in Jerusalem). The Greek angelos means messenger and is used of human messengers (Matthew 11:10; Luke 7:24; James 2:25). The trumpet also recalls the Jubilee trumpet proclaiming release (Leviticus 25:9).

With the old temple gone, the Son of Man sends his messengers, the gospel preachers (angeloi), to gather his elect people from every nation into the new temple, the church. The great trumpet is the gospel jubilee (Isaiah 27:13; Leviticus 25:9), and Deuteronomy 30:4 is fulfilled as people from the ends of heaven are gathered in. Some partial preterists instead apply the verse to the final resurrection.
The gathering is the eschatological ingathering, resurrection and redemption of the saints at the AD 70 parousia, understood in a spiritual or covenantal rather than physical sense.

At the Second Coming, angels gather the elect, chiefly the scattered believing Jews of the tribulation and other tribulation saints, from all over the earth to enter the millennial kingdom, fulfilling Deuteronomy 30:4. This is distinct from the earlier rapture of the church.

This is the gathering of the church at Christ's posttribulational coming, with the same trumpet and angels as 1 Thessalonians 4:16 and 1 Corinthians 15:52. It shows that the elect are still on earth after the tribulation.
This is the gathering of all God's people at the final return, the resurrection and transformation of believers at the last trumpet, followed by the judgment (25:31–46).
Throughout the age Christ gathers his people from every nation; the final gathering at the end completes what the mission has been doing all along.

The trumpet is the proclamation of the finished work, the good news of release, and the gathering is the drawing of people from every direction into union with Christ. Luke's “your redemption is drawing near” speaks to the believer's freedom from the old order.
Angeloi as human messengers
Angelos is used of John the Baptist (Matthew 11:10), John's disciples (Luke 7:24) and Joshua's spies (James 2:25), so preterists argue “his messengers” can be gospel preachers.
A trumpet and an ingathering in the prophets
Isaiah 27:13 speaks of a great trumpet calling exiles to worship the Lord in Jerusalem; preterists apply this to the gospel's worldwide call once the old temple was removed.
The trumpet and gathering in Paul

Paul speaks of the trumpet of God, the descent of the Lord and the gathering of believers (1 Thessalonians 4:16–17; 2 Thessalonians 2:1), and of the last trumpet at the resurrection (1 Corinthians 15:52). Futurists and amillennialists argue Matthew 24:31 is the same event.
Whether the angels are heavenly beings gathering believers at the final return, or gospel messengers gathering the nations into the church after AD 70.
The fig tree and “this generation”

When the fig tree's branch becomes tender and puts out leaves, summer is near; so when you see all these things, you know he is near, at the very gates. “Truly I say to you, this generation will not pass away until all these things take place. Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away.”

Fig trees in Judea lose their leaves in winter and put them out in spring, so new leaves signal approaching summer. Luke adds “and all the trees” (21:29), which suggests a general nature lesson. Earlier, in Matthew 21:18–20, Jesus cursed a fig tree for having leaves but no fruit, an acted parable of judgment often linked with the temple. On the meaning of genea, see the separate “This generation” section.

“This generation” means Jesus' contemporaries, as in every other use in Matthew (especially 23:36, where judgment falls on “this generation”), and “all these things” covers everything in 24:4–31, which therefore happened by AD 70, about forty years later. The disciples (“you”) would see the signs and know the end of the old order was at the gates. Verse 35 solemnly guarantees the time statement.
Full preterists read the verse in the same way and argue that it controls the entire discourse, so that the parousia and the end of the age are included in “all these things”.

Thomas Ice and others argue that “this generation” is the generation that sees the signs just described, so that those who witness the beginning of the tribulation will see its end. Scofield took genea as “race”, meaning the Jewish nation will be preserved. Some popular writers linked the fig tree with Israel's rebirth in 1948, but many dispensational scholars reject that because the text gives no such symbolism.

Blomberg and others suggest that “all these things” refers to the signs of 24:4–28, all of which occurred or began within a generation, so the end could have come at any time thereafter; the coming itself in 24:30 is not part of “these things” but is what they signal as “near”.

Amillennialists usually take “this generation” as Jesus' contemporaries, who saw the signs of AD 70 that anticipate the end. Some, following earlier commentators, take genea as “this kind of people”, the faithless in every age, or understand “all these things” as the preliminary signs rather than the final coming.

Classic historicists such as Thomas Newton and Albert Barnes took “this generation” to mean those then living and held that the destruction of Jerusalem fulfilled the prophecy within about forty years, which they counted among the strongest proofs of Christianity.

The fig tree lesson teaches readiness to read God's hand in history in every age. Whatever its first fulfilment, Jesus' words outlast heaven and earth and keep calling each generation to watchfulness.
Matthew's consistent use of “this generation”
Every other occurrence of “this generation” in Matthew (11:16; 12:41, 42, 45; 23:36) refers to Jesus' contemporaries; 23:36 directly links judgment on “this generation” to the temple's desolation.
Forty years
The destruction came about forty years after Jesus spoke, a generation in biblical reckoning (Numbers 32:13; Psalm 95:10), the same length as Israel's wilderness generation.
“When you see all these things”
Ice argues that the demonstrative “this” points back to the generation that sees “all these things” in 24:33, so the generation is defined by the signs, not by Jesus' audience.
The coming is part of “all these things”

Futurists press the other side of the preterist argument: if 24:30 is part of “all these things” and the coming has clearly not happened visibly, then the generation must be a future one, or the whole sequence must still be future.
Whether genea means Jesus' contemporaries, the future generation that sees the signs, or the Jewish race, and whether “all these things” includes the coming in 24:30.
That day and hour: the transition debate
“But concerning that day and hour no one knows, not even the angels of heaven, nor the Son, but the Father only.”

The verse opens with peri de, “but concerning”, a phrase used in early Christian writing to introduce a new topic (compare 1 Corinthians 7:1, 25; 8:1; 12:1; 1 Thessalonians 4:9; 5:1). “That day” (singular) echoes the prophetic “day of the Lord”, whereas the preceding section spoke of “those days” (plural, 24:19, 22, 29). The confession that the Son does not know the day reflects the limitation Jesus accepted in his incarnate state.

Here the discourse turns from “these things”, which had signs and a time limit (“this generation”), to “that day”, the final coming and judgment, which has no signs and no knowable date. The shift from plural “days” to singular “day”, the new-topic marker peri de, and the change from warnings about flight to warnings about unpreparedness all signal a change of subject. France and Gentry argue for this transition, and Kik placed it at 24:35/36.

There is no transition: “that day” is the day of the parousia already described, and the parousia appears on both sides of the verse (24:27, 37, 39). Full preterists see the partial-preterist division as an arbitrary concession to creedal tradition; the timing of the day was unknown, but the generation was fixed.

There is no shift from AD 70 to the future, because the whole discourse already concerns the future. “That day” is the day of Christ's return at the end of the tribulation, whose exact time is unknown even though the signs will show it is near; some dispensationalists apply 24:36–44 to the rapture.
The verse balances the signs of 24:4–35: the signs show the coming is near, but no one can calculate the date. It is a warning against date-setting while the church watches through the tribulation.

The verse confirms that Christ's return is incalculable. Some amillennialists accept a transition here from the AD 70 material to the final coming; others see the whole discourse as interweaving the two and read 24:36 as the climax of the same answer.
The unknown hour is a permanent call to readiness: because no one knows when the end will come, every generation must live as though it might be theirs.
Peri de as a topic marker

Peri de introduces new subjects in Paul's letters (1 Corinthians 7:1; 8:1; 12:1; 1 Thessalonians 5:1), and France argues it does the same here, marking the move from the temple's fall to the final day.
Signs versus no signs

Before 24:36 the events come with clear signs and a time limit; afterwards people are going about life with no warning (24:37–39), the master returns unexpectedly (24:44, 50) and even the Son does not know the time. Preterists argue that this contrast fits two different events.
Parousia on both sides
Parousia occurs in 24:27 (before the supposed transition) and 24:37, 39 (after it), which full preterists and futurists both use to argue that the discourse speaks of one coming throughout.
Whether 24:36 marks a change of subject from AD 70 to the final coming, and if so, why the same word parousia appears on both sides.
The days of Noah: one taken, one left

The coming of the Son of Man will be like the days of Noah: people were eating, drinking and marrying until the flood came and swept them all away. Two men will be in the field, one taken and one left; two women grinding at the mill, one taken and one left. Stay awake, for you do not know the day; the Son of Man comes at an hour you do not expect, like a thief.

Grinding at the mill was women's daily work, done in pairs with a hand-mill. The flood story was the classic Jewish example of sudden universal judgment (Genesis 6–7; 1 Enoch; 2 Peter 2:5; 3:6). In 24:39 the flood “took away” (ēren) the wicked; in 24:40–41 the verb for “taken” is paralambanetai, which can mean taken along or received (as in John 14:3), but also taken away for judgment.

Most partial preterists apply this section to the final coming, which unlike AD 70 comes without warning in the middle of ordinary life. The one taken is taken away in judgment like those swept away by the flood, and the one left remains, like Noah. Some partial preterists (and earlier commentators) apply the passage to AD 70, noting that Luke 17:31–37 combines similar sayings with flight from Judea.

The days of Noah describe the generation before AD 70, carrying on as usual until judgment fell. Those taken were removed in the Roman judgment or, for some full preterists, gathered to Christ at the parousia.

Many pretribulationists apply the one-taken-one-left sayings to the rapture: believers taken to meet Christ while unbelievers are left. Others, including many dispensational scholars, apply them to the Second Coming after the tribulation, where those taken are removed in judgment (as in the flood, and Luke 17:37) and the righteous are left to enter the kingdom.

The passage describes the one posttribulational coming. Many posttribulationists argue that the one taken is taken in judgment, as the flood took the wicked away, while the one left remains to share in the kingdom; it is not a secret rapture.

The coming will be sudden and will divide people who look alike, working side by side, according to their readiness. The whole section calls the church in every age to watch, since the end will come unannounced.

Ordinary life lived without reference to God is the real danger. The coming of Christ, in each crisis and finally at the end, sorts the ready from the unready, so discipleship means constant watchfulness.

The days of Noah picture people absorbed in the outward round of life, unaware of what God is doing. One is “taken” into the reality of Christ's kingdom while another remains in the old way, and the call is to be awake to his presence now.
Taken in judgment or taken to safety?

In the flood those “taken away” were the wicked; Luke's parallel ends with the vultures gathering over the corpse (17:37), which suggests judgment. But paralambanō usually means to take someone along with oneself (Matthew 1:20; 17:1; John 14:3), which supports a gathering of believers.
No signs, ordinary life

The picture of people eating, drinking and marrying, unaware, fits a coming that is unannounced, which futurists and partial preterists alike use to distinguish this section from the sign-heralded events of 24:15–28.
Whether the one taken is removed for judgment or gathered to Christ, and whether the section describes AD 70 or the final coming.
The faithful and the wicked servant

A faithful and wise servant, put in charge of his master's household, gives food at the proper time and is blessed when the master returns. But a wicked servant who says “My master is delayed” and beats his fellow servants and drinks with drunkards will be surprised by the master's return, cut in pieces and assigned a place with the hypocrites, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.

Household stewards (oikonomoi), often slaves, managed large estates for absent owners, a familiar arrangement in Roman Palestine. “Hypocrites” is Matthew's word for the scribes and Pharisees in chapter 23. The theme of delay (chronizei) recurs in 25:5 and 25:19.

Most partial preterists read 24:45–51 as part of the teaching on the final coming after the transition at 24:36. Some note that the wicked servant who abuses fellow servants resembles the leaders condemned in Matthew 23, so the parable first warned Israel's stewards, and then the church's leaders, to be faithful.
The master returned within the lifetime of the servants addressed, in AD 70, and the judgment on the wicked servant fell on the unfaithful leaders of that generation.
The parable applies the coming to the conduct of those who profess to serve the Lord, especially during the tribulation, and more broadly to believers' faithfulness before Christ returns.
The parable shows that Jesus expected a possibly long interval before his return (“my master is delayed”), during which church leaders must feed the household faithfully.
The parable describes Christian leaders in the whole period between the comings. The servant's assumption of delay is not wrong in itself; his error is to treat delay as licence.
Every age has faithful and unfaithful stewards in the church; the master's return, whenever it comes, will reveal which each one is.
The motif of delay
The wicked servant's “my master is delayed” (24:48), the bridegroom's delay (25:5) and the master's return “after a long time” (25:19) suggest Jesus envisaged an extended interval before his coming.
Hypocrites and abusive stewards
The judgment “with the hypocrites” echoes the woes of Matthew 23, which end in judgment on “this generation” (23:36), so some preterists see a first-century application to Israel's leaders.
Whether the parable's emphasis on delay points to a long interval before the final coming, and to whom the servants refer.
The ten virgins and the talents

Ten bridesmaids wait for a delayed bridegroom; five wise ones bring extra oil and go in to the wedding feast, while five foolish ones are shut out: “Watch, for you know neither the day nor the hour.” Then a master entrusts talents to three servants and, “after a long time”, settles accounts, rewarding the two who traded and casting out the one who buried his talent.

Wedding processions often took place at night, with the bridegroom fetching his bride and friends lighting the way with torches or lamps. A talent was a very large sum, roughly the wages of a labourer for many years. Luke's parable of the minas is told because people “supposed the kingdom of God was to appear immediately” (Luke 19:11), and it includes a nobleman who goes to a far country to receive a kingdom.

These parables follow the transition at 24:36 and concern readiness for the final coming and judgment after an indefinite delay. A minority apply them first to Israel's readiness for the crisis of the 60s, but most partial preterists, like most interpreters, see them as teaching for the church until the end.
The bridegroom came and the master settled accounts in AD 70: the faithful entered the kingdom while unfaithful Israel was shut out. The delay was real but within a generation.

The virgins illustrate the readiness required of Israel during the tribulation before Christ's return to establish the kingdom (the wedding feast); the talents describe the judgment of the living at the beginning of the millennial kingdom. Many dispensationalists also apply both parables to Christians more generally.
Both parables assume a long interval (“after a long time”) and call the church to prepared, productive faithfulness until the visible return, when rewards and exclusion follow.
The parables describe the church in the present age, a mixed body of wise and foolish, faithful and unfaithful, whose true state will be revealed at the final coming.
Readiness is not a matter of calculating dates but of spiritual reality (oil) and faithful use of gifts (talents). The parables address every generation.

The oil is the life of the Spirit that cannot be borrowed, and the talent is the grace entrusted to each believer. The one who buried his talent feared a hard master; the faithful knew his generosity and lived from it.
“After a long time”

The master returns after a long time (25:19), and Luke's parable corrects those who expected the kingdom to appear immediately (Luke 19:11), which many argue shows Jesus anticipated a substantial interval before his coming.
Delay but within limits?
Preterists reply that a generation of about forty years was itself a long time for disciples expecting an immediate kingdom, so the delay motif does not necessarily point beyond the first century.
Whether the parables of delay point to a long interval before the final coming, or to a delay within the first generation.
The sheep and the goats

When the Son of Man comes in his glory with all his angels, he will sit on his glorious throne and gather all the nations, separating people as a shepherd separates sheep from goats. Those who cared for “the least of these my brothers” inherit the kingdom; the others go away into eternal punishment, and the righteous into eternal life.

Palestinian shepherds commonly grazed sheep and goats together by day and separated them at night. The scene draws on Daniel 7:9–14 (the throne and the Son of Man), Zechariah 14:5 (“all the holy ones with him”) and Joel 3:2, 12 (God gathering the nations for judgment). The phrase “eternal life” and “eternal punishment” (25:46) echo Daniel 12:2, the resurrection of the righteous and the wicked.

This is the final judgment at Christ's bodily return, which partial preterists distinguish clearly from AD 70; some see 25:31 as the point where the discourse definitively moves from the first-century crisis to the end of history. The parallel with Daniel 12:2 and the universal scope (“all the nations”) mark it as the last judgment.

The judgment of the nations took place in the spiritual realm at the AD 70 parousia, when Christ began to reign over all nations and the righteous entered the kingdom. Critics note that this requires reading “eternal life” and “eternal punishment” in a non-final way that the creeds reject.

This is the judgment of the living Gentile nations at Christ's return after the tribulation, to determine who enters the millennial kingdom; “my brothers” are Jesus' Jewish brothers, the believing remnant, whose treatment reveals the nations' hearts. It is distinct from the great white throne judgment of Revelation 20:11–15.

Historic premillennialists usually see this as a picture of judgment at Christ's return, though some place the final judgment of all the dead after the millennium (Revelation 20:11–15) and treat this as a judgment of the living.

This is the one general judgment of all people at the single return of Christ, followed immediately by the eternal state. There is no room for an intervening millennium, since the righteous go straight into eternal life and the wicked into eternal punishment.
The scene reveals that how people treat Christ's needy brothers and sisters is how they treat Christ, a truth that shapes life in every age and will be made public at the end.

The Son of Man on his throne is Christ revealed in glory, and the separation exposes whether people have received the life of Christ that shows itself in love for the least. Union with him, not performance, is what the sheep did not even notice they possessed.
Universal judgment and eternal destinies

The judgment of “all the nations” issuing in eternal life and eternal punishment (25:46) mirrors Daniel 12:2 and John 5:28–29, which most interpreters, including partial preterists, read as the final resurrection and judgment.
Who are “the least of these”?

Some read “my brothers” as Christ's disciples or missionaries (compare 10:40–42; 12:48–50), others as any needy person; dispensationalists add the Jewish remnant. The identification affects whether the passage is about mission, compassion or Israel.
Whether this is the general final judgment, a judgment of the living nations before a millennium, or a covenantal judgment in AD 70.
Before the Son of Man comes: the towns of Israel

Sending out the Twelve, Jesus warns that they will be persecuted and says: “When they persecute you in one town, flee to the next, for truly I say to you, you will not have gone through all the towns of Israel before the Son of Man comes.” The saying sits in a mission discourse that also predicts councils, floggings and governors (10:17–18), language that reappears in the Olivet Discourse. Albert Schweitzer famously thought it showed Jesus expected the end during that first mission and was mistaken, which makes the verse a test case for every view.

The disciples' mission to Israel would not be complete before the Son of Man came in judgment on Jerusalem in AD 70. The persecutions of 10:17–23 match those of Matthew 24:9–13, and the coming is the same Daniel 7 coming in judgment and vindication.
The verse sets a firm limit on the parousia within the lifetime of the Twelve, and full preterists use it to argue that the one and only Second Coming happened in AD 70.
